topics.title: Government and Parliament
facts: The UK is a constitutional monarchy: the monarch is the head of state, but Parliament makes the laws and the government runs the country.
The UK Parliament meets in the Palace of Westminster in London. It has two parts: the House of Commons and the House of Lords.
The House of Commons is made up of MPs (Members of Parliament). Voters elect them. Each MP represents a local area called a constituency.
The House of Lords is the second chamber. Its members are not chosen in a general election. It checks and suggests changes to new laws.
The Prime Minister leads the government. This is usually the leader of the party that can win the support of the House of Commons.
When both Houses of Parliament agree a new law, the monarch gives Royal Assent, and it becomes an Act of Parliament.
Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have their own devolved parliament or assembly. This is called devolution. England is governed by the UK Parliament.
factsEasy: The UK has a monarch. The monarch is the head of state. Parliament makes the laws.
The UK Parliament is in London, in the Palace of Westminster. It has two parts: the House of Commons and the House of Lords.
In the House of Commons there are MPs. Voters choose them. Each MP speaks for one local area.
The House of Lords is the second part. People do not vote for its members in a general election. It checks new laws.
The Prime Minister leads the government. This is usually the leader of the biggest party.
When both parts of Parliament agree a new law, the monarch signs it. This is called Royal Assent.
Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have their own parliament or assembly. England does not. England uses the UK Parliament.

topics.title: Elections and voting
facts: A general election chooses the MPs in the House of Commons. There must be one at least every five years.
Voting is secret. You mark a ballot paper at a polling station, or you can vote by post if you are registered to do so.
To vote, you must be on the electoral register. You have to register before you can vote.
Each MP is elected for one constituency. The party that can win the support of the Commons usually forms the government.
Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland also elect their own parliament or assembly. In England, people also vote in local council elections.
At the time of writing the voting age for UK general elections is 18. The government has proposed lowering it to 16, so check gov.uk for the current rule.
factsEasy: A general election chooses the MPs. It happens at least every five years.
Voting is secret. You mark a paper at a polling station. Some people vote by post.
You must register to vote. You go on the electoral register.
Each MP speaks for one local area. The party with most support in the Commons usually runs the government.
Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland also vote for their own parliament or assembly. Everyone also votes in local elections.
For general elections the voting age is 18 now. The government wants to change it to 16. Check gov.uk.

topics.title: Values, rights and the law
facts: Fundamental British values include democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, and mutual respect and tolerance of different faiths and beliefs.
The rule of law means that everyone must obey the law, including the government and the police.
Courts decide if someone has broken the law. In a crown court in England and Wales, a jury of 12 people decides in serious cases.
In an emergency, call 999 or 112 for the police, fire service, ambulance or coastguard. Call 101 to report a crime that is not an emergency.
People have the right to say what they think, to follow a religion or none, and to be treated fairly. They must also respect the rights of others.
The minimum age to buy alcohol in a shop in the UK is 18.
factsEasy: Important values in the UK are democracy, the rule of law, freedom, and respect for people with different beliefs.
The rule of law means everyone must follow the law. This includes the government.
Courts decide if someone broke the law. In serious cases in England and Wales, 12 people called a jury decide.
In an emergency, call 999 or 112. To report a crime that is not an emergency, call 101.
You can say what you think. You can follow a religion or no religion. You must respect other people's rights.
You must be 18 to buy alcohol in a shop.

topics.title: Key dates in UK history
facts: 1066: William of Normandy won the Battle of Hastings and became king of England.
1215: King John agreed to Magna Carta. It limited the power of the king and is an important step towards the rule of law.
1666: The Great Fire of London destroyed much of the old city.
1707: The Act of Union joined England and Scotland as the Kingdom of Great Britain. Wales was already joined with England.
1914 to 1918: The First World War. 1939 to 1945: The Second World War. In 1940 the Royal Air Force won the Battle of Britain in the air.
1948: The National Health Service (NHS) was founded.
1999: The Scottish Parliament and the Welsh Assembly (now the Senedd) met for the first time after devolution.
factsEasy: 1066: William of Normandy won the Battle of Hastings. He became king of England.
1215: King John agreed to Magna Carta. After that, the king had less power.
1666: A big fire destroyed much of London. It is called the Great Fire of London.
1707: England and Scotland joined to make Great Britain. This was the Act of Union.
There were two world wars: 1914 to 1918 and 1939 to 1945. In 1940 the Royal Air Force won the Battle of Britain.
1948: The NHS began. The NHS is the UK health service.
1999: Scotland and Wales got their own parliament and assembly for the first time.

topics.title: Everyday life and services
facts: The currency of the UK is the pound sterling (£). Some banks in Scotland and Northern Ireland print their own banknotes.
The NHS gives health care. To see a family doctor (GP), register with a GP practice near where you live.
In the UK, vehicles drive on the left. The Highway Code is the official book of rules and advice for road users.
Many households pay council tax to their local council to help pay for local services such as rubbish collection.
On Remembrance Sunday, many people wear a red poppy to remember people who died in wars.
Public holidays in the UK are called bank holidays. They are not the same in every nation.

topics.title: The four nations
facts: The UK is made up of four nations: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The capital of the UK is London.
The capitals are London (England), Edinburgh (Scotland), Cardiff (Wales) and Belfast (Northern Ireland).
Patron saints: St David (Wales) 1 March, St Patrick (Ireland) 17 March, St George (England) 23 April, St Andrew (Scotland) 30 November.
The Union Flag combines the crosses of St George (England), St Andrew (Scotland) and St Patrick (Ireland). Wales is not shown separately on it.
Scotland has the Scottish Parliament at Holyrood, Wales has the Senedd in Cardiff, and Northern Ireland has the Northern Ireland Assembly at Stormont.
The Isle of Man and the Channel Islands are not part of the UK.
factsEasy: The UK has four nations: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The capital of the UK is London.
The capital cities are London, Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast.
Each nation has a patron saint: Wales St David (1 March), Ireland St Patrick (17 March), England St George (23 April), Scotland St Andrew (30 November).
The Union Flag is the flag of the UK. It joins the crosses of England, Scotland and Ireland. Wales is not on it.
Scotland has a parliament in Edinburgh. Wales has the Senedd in Cardiff. Northern Ireland has an Assembly in Belfast.
The Isle of Man and the Channel Islands are not part of the UK.
